title: Question 5
stem:
A horizontal string is stretched between two fixed points A and B. A vibrator is used to oscillate the string and produce an observable stationary wave.

At one instant, the moving string is straight, as shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

The dots in the diagram represent the positions of the nodes on the string. Point P on the string is moving downwards.

The wave on the string has a speed of $35\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and a period of $0.040\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Explain how the stationary wave is formed on the string.

markscheme_points.text: wave(s) (travel along string and) reflect at fixed point / A / B / end ;
incident and reflected waves superpose / interfere or two waves travelling / with speed in opposite directions superpose

hints: Hint 1: Think about what must happen when a travelling wave running along the string reaches a fixed point like A or B that cannot move.
Hint 2: Think about what happens when two identical waves travelling in opposite directions overlap on the same string.
parts.proper_answer: Waves travelling along the string are reflected at the fixed ends A and B. The incident and reflected waves travelling in opposite directions superpose to form a stationary wave.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Reflection at the Fixed Ends**
You have a progressive wave sent out by the vibrator. When it hits a point that cannot move, like A or B, it cannot pass through, so it is reflected back along the string. You now have waves travelling both ways at the same speed and frequency.

Step 2: **Superposition to Give a Stationary Wave**
Where the two oppositely travelling waves overlap they add together by the principle of superposition. In some places they always cancel to give nodes of zero displacement, and in other places they reinforce to give antinodes. The resulting pattern does not travel, it is a stationary wave.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: On Fig. 5.1, sketch a line to show a possible position of the string a quarter of a cycle later than the position shown in the diagram.

markscheme_points.text: line has an approximate sinusoidal shape with maximum down

hints: Hint 1: The string is straight now, so every particle except the nodes is moving at maximum speed. Since point P is moving down, think about which way each loop must move to reach its extreme displacement a quarter of a cycle later.
parts.proper_answer: Approximate sine wave through all nodes with maximum displacement downwards in the first loop from A.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From Straight to Extreme**
A straight string in a stationary wave means zero displacement everywhere, so all antinodes are passing through equilibrium at maximum speed. A quarter of a period later they all reach maximum displacement.

Step 2: **Which Way Up?**
Point P is in the first loop from A and is moving downwards, so that whole loop moves down to a trough. Adjacent loops always move in opposite directions, so the sketch is a smooth sinusoidal curve through the fixed nodes, down, up, down, up, down along the string.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Determine the horizontal distance from A to B.
hints: Hint 1: Start with the numbers $35\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $0.040\text{ s}$. In one full period, how far does a wave crest travel along the string?
Hint 2: Use $v = f\lambda$ with $f = 1/T$ to calculate the wavelength $\lambda$ of the travelling waves.
Hint 3: Count the number of half-wavelength loops between A and B in Fig. 5.1 and multiply by $\lambda/2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Wavelength**
The travelling waves obey the wave equation. With frequency $f = 1/T$: $$v = f\lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$ Rearranged for wavelength: $$\lambda = vT$$ Put in the numbers: $$\lambda = 35 \times 0.040 = 1.4\text{ m}$$

Step 2: **Count How Many Wavelengths Fit in AB**
Between two adjacent nodes is half a wavelength, $\lambda/2$. From Fig. 5.1 there are 5 loops between A and B, so: $$AB = 5 \times \frac{\lambda}{2} = 2.5\lambda$$

Step 3: **Calculate AB**
$$AB = 2.5 \times 1.4 = 3.5\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
A particle on the string has zero displacement at time $t = 0$. From time $t = 0$ to time $t = 0.060\text{ s}$, the particle moves through a total distance of $72\text{ mm}$.

Calculate the amplitude of oscillation of the particle.
hints: Hint 1: Compare the time interval $0.060\text{ s}$ with the period $0.040\text{ s}$ to work out how many full cycles, including any half cycle, the particle completes.
Hint 2: Remember that starting from zero displacement, the particle travels one amplitude in a quarter period, so one full period is four amplitudes.
parts.proper_answer: Number of cycles $= 0.060/0.040 = 1.5$, total distance $= 6 \times$ amplitude, amplitude $= 72/6 = 12\text{ mm}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **How Many Oscillations?**
Number of periods in the time interval: $$n = \frac{t}{T} = \frac{0.060}{0.040} = 1.5$$ So the particle makes one and a half full oscillations.

Step 2: **Link Total Path to Amplitude**
Let amplitude be $a$. From equilibrium to extreme is $a$ in a quarter period. A full period is four such journeys: $$\text{distance per period} = 4a$$ For 1.5 periods: $$\text{total distance} = 1.5 \times 4a = 6a$$ Hence: $$6a = 72\text{ mm}$$ $$a = 12\text{ mm}$$
